r: This course introduces Trauma-Informed Care for first responders: defining TIC, modifying agency interventions to increase client safety, applying trauma-informed practice with diverse populations including those with PTSD, and identifying strategies for managing vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue. The applied work mixes conceptual knowledge transmission, which AI already explains fluently, with relational judgment about vulnerable, trauma-affected people, where a misapplied intervention can retraumatize a client. Task-exposure research finds interpersonal, judgment-laden work less exposed than pure information delivery, and the self-monitoring skills around vicarious trauma are not something a model can build for a learner. No licensure or accreditation mandate governs this elective, so the binding constraint is the verification burden inherent in trauma-sensitive practice rather than external credentialing. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop this relational competence remains intact.

By 2031, AI tools will competently draft TIC training materials, screening checklists, and explanatory content about PTSD and compassion fatigue, further eroding the pure information-transmission portion of the course. Observed-usage data shows office and explanatory tasks are heavily represented in current AI use, pushing base automatability upward. But the course's distinctive value is judgment about how to modify a real interaction with a distressed person, and the jagged-frontier evidence indicates that outside a model's competence zone, users relying on AI without underlying knowledge are measurably less accurate — precisely the risk in trauma-sensitive contact. That verification burden keeps a knowledgeable human in the loop and dampens the rating one band below where raw task exposure alone would place it. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting real erosion of the informational content, not of the relational core.

A decade out, generative systems will likely produce sophisticated, individualized guidance on trauma-informed approaches, and adoption in human-services and first-responder agencies will be considerably more widespread than today, per diffusion trends described in Census BTOS data, even though such adoption still lags raw model capability. Even so, the central case still requires a first responder or human-services worker who personally recognizes trauma responses, applies safety-oriented modifications in real time, and manages their own vicarious trauma — capacities that are practiced, not simply informed by reading material. No licensure lock protects this course, so its durability rests entirely on the verification-heavy, relational nature of trauma-sensitive work. The rating holds Medium; the wide uncertainty concerns how much of the didactic content shifts to AI-assisted delivery, not whether the relational competence remains instrumentally necessary for practice.
FER 1020.d: Students will be introduced to the concept of Trauma- Informed Care (TIC) and how agencies, Human Services professionals, and first responders can utilize this model to benefit clients. Students will describe and define what TIC is and ways in which traditional interventions can be modified to increase the sense of safety experienced by clients and those who work with them. Students will learn how to incorporate trauma-informed practices into interventions with diverse populations, especially those with Post- Traumatic Injury and/or Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Students will also examine strategies for identifying and managing vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue.

r: Applications of Fire Research trains students to examine research principles and methodology and to conduct and evaluate independent research across fire dynamics, test standards and codes, fire modeling, structural fire safety, firefighter health and safety, and risk analysis, capped by a service-learning project. Literature synthesis and methodology description are squarely in the writing-and-research category that observed-usage data shows AI already handles heavily, and drafting research summaries is a highly exposed task. But evaluating whether a piece of fire-safety research is methodologically sound, and applying it to real fire-protection decisions, carries a genuine error cost: bad research application can inform unsafe codes or practices. That verification burden dampens the rating at 24 months even as the drafting mechanics of research writing are already largely automatable.

By 2031, AI research assistants will retrieve, summarize, and synthesize fire-science literature with real fluency, and GDPval-style evaluations suggest AI-produced research deliverables will approach, though not yet fully match, expert quality on complex applied work of this specialized kind. The course's instrumental center shifts from producing the literature review to critically evaluating whether an AI-synthesized research summary is methodologically sound before it informs a fire-protection decision — exactly the jagged-frontier problem where confident but wrong synthesis is dangerous and hard to detect without domain knowledge. No accreditation body locks this course's credit hours in place, so nothing structurally protects it beyond that verification role. The rating rises to Medium: drafting automates, but the applied judgment the service-learning project builds does not.

A decade out, AI systems will plausibly conduct much of the literature retrieval, synthesis, and even preliminary analysis for fire-related research questions, and diffusion into fire-service agencies will likely be more complete than today's uneven adoption, though still probably short of universal. The central case still requires someone who can specify a sound research question, judge the credibility of an AI-generated synthesis against fire-dynamics fundamentals, and apply findings to real risk-reduction and code decisions where consequences are physical and public. That verification role, not any institutional lock, is what keeps the rating from reaching High. The uncertainty is genuine about how much of the analytical workflow AI absorbs, but the human oversight function this course builds appears durable through 2036.
FER 3000.d: The students will examine the basic principles of research and methodology for analyzing current fire-related research. The course also provides a framework for conducting and evaluating independent research in the following areas: fire dynamics, fire test standards and codes, fire safety, fire modeling, structural fire safety, life safety, firefighter health and safety, automatic detection and suppression, transportation fire hazards, risk analysis and loss control, fire service applied research, and new trends in fire-related research. Successful completion of the course will require participation in a service learning project.

r: This course builds a theoretical framework for the ethical, sociological, organizational, political, and legal components of community risk reduction, and a methodology for developing a comprehensive community risk reduction plan. The applied work is analytical and document-centered: synthesizing demographic and hazard data, applying a planning framework, and producing a written plan — activities that sit inside the computer-and-analytical categories observed-usage data identifies as the largest current AI use case. Professional-writing research shows large time savings and quality gains when AI assists structured document drafting, which directly applies to plan development. No licensure or clinical component embodies this work; it is fully digital planning and policy analysis. At 24 months the instrumental need is already meaningfully eroded, since AI can competently draft framework-based risk-reduction plans.

By 2031, AI planning tools will plausibly integrate hazard, demographic, and code data to generate draft community risk-reduction plans with modest human editing, extending the productivity gains professional-writing research already documents for structured analytical documents of this kind. Diffusion data suggests such tools will be more broadly adopted in public-safety agencies than they are today, though unevenly and behind raw capability. The course's applied tasks — framework synthesis and plan authorship — are exactly the kind of writing-and-analysis work task-exposure research classifies as highly exposed, and no accreditation or licensure floor protects the credit hours. The rating rises to High: the instrumental case for a student personally constructing these plans weakens substantially as AI absorbs both the analytical framing and the drafting.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems producing sophisticated, data-integrated risk-reduction plans largely autonomously, with human planners shifting toward specifying local priorities and validating outputs against community context and lived experience on the ground. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that writing and analytical synthesis are strongly associated with exposure applies directly here, and nothing in the institutional landscape — no licensure gate, no accreditation credit-hour floor — holds this course's necessity in place. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much local political and ethical judgment resists full automation, since community priorities are contested and value-laden in ways a model cannot adjudicate alone. The rating holds High, with that judgment residue as the honest caveat rather than a basis for a lower band.
FER 3110.d: Students will be introduced to a theoretical framework for understanding the ethical, sociological, organizational, political, and legal components of community risk reduction and a methodology for the development of a comprehensive community risk reduction plan.

r: Fire and Emergency Services Administration is a management primer covering persuasion and influence, accountable budgeting, anticipating organizational change, analytical management tools, and building internal and external cooperation toward a department's mission. These map onto general management activities — coordinating work, guiding subordinates, budgeting, and organizational analysis — that observed-usage data shows are already well represented in AI-assisted knowledge work, particularly office and administrative tasks. Budget analysis, memo drafting, and change-management frameworks are all things AI performs competently today. There is no licensure or clinical embodiment protecting this course, and no accreditation credit-hour floor mandates it. At 24 months the instrumental case for teaching these administrative frameworks by hand is already meaningfully eroded, since much of the content is document- and analysis-based generalist management knowledge.

By 2031, AI will plausibly draft budgets, model organizational change scenarios, and generate persuasive internal communications with real competence, consistent with the enterprise API data showing automation-oriented use, not just augmentation, dominates business tasks of this administrative kind. The course's leadership-development core — building internal and external cooperation, exercising judgment about people and politics within a fire department — resists full automation less because of technical difficulty and more because it involves situated organizational trust that a model cannot substitute for a human occupying the role. No institutional lock caps the erosion. The rating rises to High: the administrative and analytical substance of the course is substantially automatable, even though the interpersonal leadership function retains real value for whoever holds the position.

A decade out, the central case has AI handling most routine fire-department administrative analysis — budgeting scenarios, staffing models, compliance tracking — leaving human leaders to exercise judgment, build relationships, and make final accountable decisions on behalf of their department. Task-exposure research's finding that programming and administrative-writing tasks are strongly exposed applies to much of this course's content, and no accreditation or licensure mandate holds it in place. The uncertainty is real about how quickly fire departments themselves adopt these tools, since diffusion research shows adoption lagging capability even where technically feasible. The rating holds High, reflecting that the instrumental need to personally master these administrative frameworks — as opposed to directing AI-assisted versions of them — is substantially diminished.
FER 3140.d: This course is designed to be a progressive primer for students who want more knowledge about fire and emergency services administration. Students will examine the following skills necessary to manage and lead a fire and emergency services department through the challenges and changes of the 21st century: Persuasion and influence, accountable budgeting, anticipation of challenges and the need for change, and using specific management tools for analyzing and solving problems. A central part of the course focuses on how the leadership of a fire and emergency services department develops internal and external cooperation to create a coordinated approach to achieving the department's mission.

r: This course examines the factors shaping fire risk and the tools of fire prevention — risk-reduction education, codes and standards, inspection and plans review, fire investigation, master planning, and program strategy — alongside the evolving role of the fire-prevention professional in managing prevention programs. Codes-and-standards research, plans review, and program administration are document- and analysis-heavy tasks that map onto categories observed-usage data shows are already common AI use, and a plans-review checklist against a code is a highly structured task AI performs well. A modest field-inspection component keeps some of this embodied, tempering but not eliminating exposure. No licensure or accreditation floor protects the course. At 24 months the instrumental case for the administrative and code-analysis content is already meaningfully eroded.

By 2031, AI will plausibly perform first-pass plans review, code-compliance checks, and prevention-program analysis with real competence, extending the productivity gains professional-writing research documents for structured analytical work into this fire-code domain and its adjacent regulatory paperwork and official correspondence with the public. Diffusion data suggests fire and building departments will adopt such tools unevenly but meaningfully by this horizon, trailing the underlying capability curve considerably as agencies retool. The course's remaining core — exercising judgment about ambiguous or novel code-compliance situations and coordinating prevention strategy with communities and officials — carries more nuance than an automated checklist, but the administrative bulk of the content is squarely exposed. No accreditation credit-hour floor caps the erosion. The rating rises to High.

A decade out, the central case has AI handling routine code compliance, plans-review triage, and prevention-program documentation largely autonomously, with fire-prevention professionals concentrating on complex site judgment, community engagement, and final regulatory sign-off on public-safety matters of real consequence to residents. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that structured document analysis is strongly exposed applies directly to much of this course, and no institutional lock — no licensure, no accreditation floor — holds the course's instrumental necessity in place. Genuine uncertainty remains about how much physical inspection persists as a human task even as documentary review automates, since a building's actual condition still needs eyes on it. The rating holds High, anchored by the administrative and code-analysis core rather than the inspection residue.
FER 3200.d: In this course, students will examine the factors that shape fire risk and the tools for fire prevention, including risk reduction education, codes and standards, inspection and plans review, fire investigation, research, master planning, various types of influences, and strategies. Also, students will examine the changing roles and responsibilities of fire prevention professionals in managing fire prevention programs and risk reduction activities to ensure public safety.

r: Understanding International Terrorism surveys the history and evolution of international terrorism on a global scale, develops a comparative perspective, and asks students to critically evaluate counterterrorism methods and theorize terrorist motivations — an analytical, historical, essay-driven course with no clinical, field, or licensure component. This is squarely knowledge-exposure territory: task-exposure research finds writing and explanatory synthesis strongly and positively associated with AI exposure, and a model can already produce competent historical summaries and comparative counterterrorism analysis on demand. There is no GT-Pathways designation or accreditation mandate protecting this elective in the catalog record, and it does not scaffold a required later sequence. At 24 months the instrumental case for a student personally producing this analytical content, rather than directing and checking an AI-generated version, is already substantially eroded.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate historically grounded, well-sourced analyses of terrorism's evolution and comparative counterterrorism policy, sharpening the question of why a student must construct this content unaided rather than direct it. The course's residue is critical evaluation — judging whether a given counterterrorism argument holds up, since observed-usage data shows AI writing is already pervasive in explanatory tasks and this course produces exactly that kind of output. No institutional lock — no gen-ed mandate, no foundational role in a required sequence, no accreditation floor — caps the erosion. The rating rises to High: the course's applied tasks sit in a highly automatable, unprotected knowledge domain, even as engaging directly with primary historical and policy sources retains pedagogical value.

A decade out, AI will plausibly be a highly capable interlocutor and synthesizer on terrorism history and counterterrorism policy, and the central case has students routinely using such tools to explore the material rather than compiling it from scratch through independent library research and archival work. Nothing structural — no licensure, no transfer mandate, no scaffolding role for later required coursework — holds the course's instrumental necessity above what its knowledge-exposure profile implies. The genuine uncertainty concerns how contested, evolving geopolitical judgment resists full automation even as factual synthesis is automated, since assessing current terrorist threats involves interpreting ambiguous, fast-moving information. The rating holds High, reflecting that this is a knowledge-transmission and analysis course without a binding institutional or verification-based floor.
FER 3300.d: This course will enable students to understand the evolution and current state of international terrorism by examining its history on a global scale. This global perspective will provide students with the ability to think sensibly about international terrorism and critically evaluate which counterterrorism methods have proven to be effective. Additionally, this course will investigate the theory behind the international terrorist's motivations and actions.

r: Introduction to Homeland Security surveys the components of homeland security, the agencies and their inter-related duties, the historical events that shaped the field, and the state, national, and international laws and threats — especially terrorism — confronting it. This is an informational survey course: identifying agencies, summarizing legal frameworks, and explaining historical developments are exactly the explanatory synthesis tasks that AI performs competently and that task-exposure research classifies as highly exposed. No embodied, clinical, or field component is described, no GT-Pathways or accreditation designation appears in the catalog record, and the course does not function as scaffolding for a required later sequence. At 24 months, the instrumental case for a student personally compiling this survey knowledge, versus directing an AI-generated version of it, is already meaningfully weakened.

By 2031, AI systems will plausibly generate accurate, well-organized overviews of the homeland-security agency landscape, its legal architecture, and its threat environment on demand, extending today's already-strong performance on explanatory synthesis of this survey kind of content. Observed-usage data shows this kind of informational-writing task is a large and growing share of current AI use across knowledge domains generally. Without a transfer mandate, accreditation floor, or foundational role protecting the course's credit hours, the erosion is not capped. The residual instrumental value is critical evaluation of competing homeland-security policy claims — a genuine but comparatively thin protection against an otherwise highly exposed body of survey content. The rating rises to High, tracking the course's informational character rather than any binding institutional constraint.

A decade out, AI will plausibly serve as an authoritative, interactive explainer of homeland-security structures, law, and threat trends, and the central case has that capability broadly diffused into education by this horizon even if actual agency adoption itself still lags well behind the frontier. Nothing in the institutional record — no licensure gate, no gen-ed lock, no accreditation credit-hour requirement — holds this course's necessity above what its exposure profile implies. The honest uncertainty is how much evolving, politically contested threat assessment resists clean automation even as the descriptive survey content is fully AI-deliverable. The rating holds High, anchored in the course's status as an unprotected knowledge-transmission survey rather than a course with a binding verification or institutional floor.
FER 3330.d: This course will enable the student to identify the important components of homeland security. The student will recognize the agencies associated with homeland security and their inter-related duties and relationships. The student will explore the historical events that have impacted homeland security, the state, national, and international laws affecting homeland security, and the most critical threats, especially terrorism, confronting homeland security.

r: Personnel Development for Fire and Emergency Services covers personnel administration and human-resource management within fire and emergency-service organizations: personnel management, organizational development, productivity, recruitment and selection, performance-management systems, discipline, and collective bargaining. Much of this is HR administration — policy drafting, performance-review documentation, recruitment materials — that maps onto office and administrative tasks observed-usage data shows are already heavily AI-assisted, and enterprise API data shows this category skews toward automation rather than augmentation. Discipline and collective-bargaining judgment retain a real interpersonal and negotiation component, but no licensure or clinical embodiment protects the course overall. At 24 months, the instrumental case for personally producing the administrative HR content this course covers is already substantially eroded by generalist AI competence at similar tasks.

By 2031, AI will plausibly draft performance-management frameworks, recruitment materials, and disciplinary documentation with real fluency, consistent with enterprise data showing automation-heavy adoption of administrative HR-style tasks across knowledge-work sectors generally, not just fire service specifically or public safety administration broadly. Fire departments themselves will likely adopt such tools unevenly, per diffusion research showing capability outpacing actual deployment. The course's residue — negotiating collective bargaining, exercising disciplinary judgment about a specific person's conduct, and building trust within a department — involves situated interpersonal stakes a model does not carry on a human administrator's behalf, but this is a smaller share of the course's total content than the administrative-systems material. No institutional lock caps the erosion. The rating rises to High.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most of the administrative HR mechanics — policy documentation, staffing analysis, performance-system design — for fire and emergency-service organizations, leaving the negotiation and disciplinary-judgment core to a human administrator who holds accountability for the outcome and its consequences for the department and its individual members. Task-exposure research's finding that administrative and writing-heavy work is strongly exposed applies to the bulk of this course's content, and no accreditation or licensure floor holds it in place across a catalog cycle. The genuine uncertainty is how much collective-bargaining and disciplinary judgment resists automation given its adversarial, relationship-dependent character. The rating holds High, reflecting that the administrative substance dominates the course even as a smaller negotiation-judgment core persists.
FER 3430.d: In this course, students will examine relationships and issues in personnel administration and human resource management within the context of fire and emergency service organizations, including personnel management, organizational development, productivity, recruitment and selection, performance management systems, discipline, and collective bargaining.

r: Political and Legal Foundations for Fire Protection reviews the American legal system and covers legal and political issues in employment and personnel matters, administrative and operational matters, planning and code enforcement, and legislative processes affecting the fire service, aiming to develop fire administrators as effective risk managers who can find and apply appropriate legal rules. Legal-research and issue-spotting tasks are well represented in current AI use, and professional-writing research shows large gains when AI assists structured legal-adjacent document work. Applying legal rules to specific fire-service situations carries real liability consequences, giving this course more genuine verification weight than a pure survey course, but no licensure exam or bar-style credential gates it. At 24 months the administrative-legal content is already substantially exposed.

By 2031, AI legal-research tools will plausibly identify relevant statutes, case precedent, and regulatory requirements for fire-service legal questions with real fluency, extending today's strong AI performance on legal-adjacent writing and research tasks generally across professional and regulatory domains alike, including public administration. The jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant here: a plausible-sounding but incorrect legal analysis is genuinely dangerous in liability and personnel contexts, so verifying an AI-generated legal conclusion against the underlying rules keeps a knowledgeable human necessary. That verification role is real but does not amount to an institutional lock, and it is not enough to prevent the rating from rising as the drafting and research mechanics automate. The rating moves to High, reflecting substantial erosion of the research-and-drafting core.

A decade out, AI will plausibly perform most first-pass legal-issue identification and drafting for fire-service administrative and personnel matters, with human administrators concentrating on validating conclusions before they carry legal weight for the department and its officers on the public record — precisely the oversight role the jagged-frontier evidence suggests remains valuable and necessary. No accreditation credit-hour floor or licensure exam protects this course's place in the curriculum, so its rating tracks the underlying task-exposure profile rather than any institutional floor. The honest uncertainty is how much this verification role still requires the full depth of legal-foundations coursework versus a narrower AI-oversight module taught later. The rating holds High, anchored in the strongly exposed research-and-drafting content that dominates the course.
FER 3460.d: In this course, students will examine the legal aspects of the fire service and the political and social impacts of legal issues. The course includes a review of the American legal system and in- depth coverage of legal and political issues involving employment and personnel matters, administrative and operational matters, planning and code enforcement, and legislative and political processes with regard to the fire service. At the end of the course students will be able to understand how fire and emergency services administrators perform as effective risk managers by recognizing legal and political issues affecting public safety, and finding and applying appropriate legal rules and/or political constructs as indicated.

r: Fire Service Ethics examines the basic principles of ethics as applied to fire-service operations and management, with attention to current issues in the fire service — an applied-ethics course built on evaluating arguments about right conduct in specific organizational situations, not on generating explanatory prose. Task-exposure research consistently finds critical-thinking and evaluative-reasoning tasks among the least exposed categories, even though AI can produce fluent ethical commentary. The course's purpose is a student's own capacity to weigh competing values and judge a specific fire-service scenario, which is exactly the kind of judgment that AI output cannot substitute without a human able to check whether the reasoning is actually sound. No accreditation or licensure mandate governs this course; the binding constraint is the reasoning task itself. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact.

By 2031, AI will produce fluent, well-structured ethical analysis of fire-service scenarios, sharpening the surface-level tension around the writing artifact rather than the underlying quality of the reasoning itself. But evaluating whether a given ethical argument about a use-of-force, personnel-discipline, or resource-allocation situation is actually sound — distinguishing a persuasive rationalization from a defensible judgment — is a verification-heavy task, and the jagged-frontier evidence shows users outside a model's reliable zone are measurably less accurate while remaining overconfident. That dynamic keeps a human who can independently reason through the ethics necessary, and dampens the rating a full band below where the underlying task automatability alone would place it. The rating stays Low, reflecting the durability of applied ethical reasoning as a protected competence.

A decade out, AI will plausibly be a capable interlocutor on fire-service ethics, able to generate persuasive positions on any organizational dilemma, and the central case has broader integration of such tools into professional training. Even so, the human capacity to critically evaluate an ethical argument — including one an AI produces — remains the substrate the course builds, and that verification-heavy reasoning task is precisely what science and critical-thinking-intensive work is found to resist in exposure research. No institutional lock protects this course; its durability rests entirely on the reasoning task's resistance to automation. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that how ethics instruction is delivered, rather than whether the reasoning competence is needed, is what may change most.
FER 3800.d: This course examines the basic principles of ethics as related to fire service operations and management with special attention given to current issues in the fire service.

r: This course applies social-power, class, and subcultural analysis to first-responder community relations, mapping to Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships and Communicating with Persons Outside Organization. Assignments center on written evaluation of how first responders navigate cultural friction and ambivalence with the communities they police, patrol, or serve during emergencies. Generative tools already draft literature summaries and structure comparative cultural analyses, and observed-usage data shows writing and office-style tasks are prominent in current consumer and enterprise deployment. But the applied work task is not the essay; it is real-time judgment during encounters with diverse, sometimes distrustful publics, where a responder's read of a cultural situation carries safety and legitimacy consequences that a model cannot supply in the moment. That interpersonal, presence-bound application keeps instrumental need for the course intact through the near term, even as drafting support spreads through written assignments.

By 2031, tools will more fluently synthesize case studies of subcultural conflict and generate discussion prompts on power and ecological patterns in community-first-responder relations, nudging analytic-writing tasks further toward augmentation. Task-exposure research classifies writing as strongly positively associated with exposure, so the paper-and-discussion scaffolding of this course is not immune. Yet the course's actual instrumental target, cultural competence exercised inside live, ambivalent field interactions, remains embodied and adversarial: misreading a community's trust dynamics has non-obvious failure modes that only a present, accountable human can catch and correct. Verification burden stays high because the cost of a bad real-time call is reputational and physical, not merely textual. Confidence in AI substituting for the applied competence itself should not rise proportionally with its fluency at producing coursework artifacts about that competence.

Ten years out, capability trend data suggests continued fast growth in what models can draft and analyze regarding cultural dynamics, but diffusion research shows adoption of such tools inside public-safety agencies lags capability and remains uneven, and macro estimates of aggregate productivity impact stay modest over a decade. It is plausible AI becomes a standard brainstorming aid for cultural-competence training content by 2036, but implausible that it displaces the course's core instrumental function: preparing responders to exercise interpersonal judgment amid social power imbalances in the field. This projection should be held loosely given how much community-relations practice and first-responder training policy could shift over a decade, but the embodied, real-time, high-consequence character of the applied skill is a structural constraint unlikely to dissolve quickly, so the course's instrumental necessity is expected to persist as Low exposure.
FER 3911.d: Students in this course examine first responder roles in society in relation to social power, class structure, ecological patterns, subcultural developments, and processes of change in the community and in the larger culture. Culture is examined in order to comprehend the interaction between subcultures in the larger society, as well as develop an understanding of cultural competence applications for first responders. Students in this course evaluate the ambivalence in the social processes of first responders, and the challenges inherent in the profession.

r: The internship places students inside actual fire and emergency-management operations, mapping to Performing General Physical Activities and Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others under direct professional supervision. The instrumental value is the supervised, embodied practice itself, applying classroom knowledge inside a real department, not a summarizable deliverable. Task-exposure research finds manual and physically situated work is consistently low-exposure, and this placement is defined by hands-on presence in a public or private emergency-services setting rather than desk-based analysis. Even where administrative sub-tasks like report drafting could see augmentation, the core requirement, being physically present, supervised, and evaluated in a working agency, cannot be replaced by a model. Confidence is tempered because internship content varies by department and is not fully specified in the catalog description, but the embodied structure itself is a firm near-term constraint.

Productivity research shows the largest AI gains accrue to novice workers on well-defined digital tasks, and an intern could plausibly use such tools to speed report writing, incident summaries, or after-action documentation by 2031. That augmentation does not touch the placement's instrumental purpose, however, which is supervised professional practice inside a physical emergency-services environment where a human supervisor verifies performance in real time. Verification burden stays firmly with the on-site supervisor, and embodiment is total: the course cannot be completed by producing text alone. Some erosion is conceivable if departments restructure internship duties toward more remote or administrative work, but nothing in the current description suggests that shift, so the instrumental need for hands-on placement should hold through the medium term with only modest change to its administrative periphery.

A decade out, capability trend data implies far more capable general-purpose systems, but diffusion research shows firm-level AI adoption still lags capability considerably even in digitally native sectors, and public-safety agencies structuring supervised practicums are unlikely to be early movers in replacing embodied training with simulation. It is possible that virtual or augmented-reality tools supplement scenario training by 2036, but the internship's defining feature, direct professional immersion evaluated by a workplace supervisor, is a governance and liability structure independent of task automatability. This is a genuinely uncertain horizon for how agencies structure trainee experience generally, and the projection should be held loosely, but nothing in the observed evidence points toward physical, supervised placement losing its instrumental necessity within this window.
FER 3980.d: Students in this course gain an internship experience in a fire and/or emergency services management setting where students are able to use the skills learned in the classroom in a supervised, professional realm. Students work as fire and emergency management practitioners in a variety of public and private outlets. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: Students apply data collection, statistics, probability, decision analysis, utility modeling, resource allocation, and cost-benefit analysis to fire and emergency-services agency problems, mapping directly to Analyzing Data or Information and Making Decisions and Solving Problems. This is quantitative, spreadsheet-and-model-centered work of exactly the kind observed-usage data flags as heaviest in current deployment, where Computer & Mathematical is the largest usage category by a wide margin. Statistical modeling, utility-function construction, and cost-benefit writeups are already within reach of current tools for well-specified problems. Verification burden is moderate rather than minimal: outputs feeding real resource-allocation decisions for a fire agency still need an analyst who understands the underlying assumptions. No licensure or clinical-hour mandate anchors this course, so near-term exposure sits at the boundary between augmentation and partial task substitution rather than untouched status.

By 2031, task-exposure research's finding that mathematicians and quantitative analysts sit among the most-exposed occupations should extend to this course's core content: applying probability, utility modeling, and cost-benefit frameworks to agency decisions. GDPval-style evaluations show frontier models already reaching parity-adjacent performance on real analytical deliverables, and productivity studies show substantial task-speed gains on structured technical work. The instrumental gap narrows further as decision-analysis templates, resource-allocation models, and statistical writeups become more directly producible by AI with light analyst oversight rather than analyst-driven construction. Verification still matters because misapplied utility models in a public-safety budget context carry real cost, but the balance of labor shifts meaningfully toward AI performing the computational core while a human validates framing and assumptions rather than building the analysis from scratch.

Capability trend data describing rapid growth in model task-time horizons supports continued movement toward AI performing most of the analytical pipeline, data collection, modeling, and cost-benefit writeup, that this course teaches by hand today. Diffusion remains the countervailing force: adoption inside public fire and emergency agencies, which are not digitally leading organizations, likely continues to lag capability, and macro productivity estimates over a decade stay modest in aggregate. A ten-year projection here should be held with real uncertainty about how quickly public-sector agencies actually adopt AI-driven decision analysis versus continuing manual practice, but on capability grounds alone the instrumental case for hand-taught statistical and utility-modeling skill is weaker than for any other course in this batch, sustaining a High rating for this horizon.
FER 4100.d: In this course, students apply the tools and techniques of rational decision making in Fire and Emergency Services agencies. Students learn and apply data collection, statistics, probability, decision analysis, utility modeling, resource allocation, and cost- benefit analysis for fire and emergency services.

r: Students learn unified command, Emergency Operations Center strategy and tactics, and disaster deployment decision-making, mapping to Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others and Making Decisions and Solving Problems under Emergency Manager duties. EOC work is real-time coordination among agencies, personnel, and evolving hazards, closer to crisis command than to document production. The jagged-frontier findings are directly relevant: outside a model's competence boundary, users relying on AI are measurably less accurate while remaining overconfident in the output, a serious risk during live disaster coordination where miscalibrated trust could cascade into operational failure. Verification burden is high because EOC decisions carry life-safety consequences and rarely have single correct answers. Near-term instrumental need for learning unified command and EOC judgment firsthand stays intact despite AI's growing usefulness for drafting plans or logs.

By 2031, AI assistance for information synthesis inside an EOC, tracking resource status, drafting situation reports, summarizing incoming feeds, will likely be more common, nudging the base automatability of supporting tasks upward. But the deterministic core of this course, exercising unified-command judgment and decision authority during a live, multi-agency disaster response, remains a real-time interpersonal and crisis-coordination activity that the jagged-frontier research suggests AI performs unevenly outside well-bounded scenarios. Verification burden stays low in the protective sense: an Emergency Manager cannot outsource accountability for command decisions to a model whose failure modes in genuinely novel disasters are not well characterized.
